## Why are we doing this? {.center-title}

David Brooks, *The Atlantic* (June 2026), on who will thrive in the AI age:

<br>

> "When intelligence is plentiful, volition is valuable."

<br>

His argument: What will separate people isn't raw intelligence — it's their **relationship to mental effort**. Today is about building the right relationship with these tools, on our terms.

::: footer-cite
Brooks, "The People Who Will Thrive in the AI Age," *The Atlantic*, June 28, 2026
:::

---

## Three kinds of AI users (per Brooks)

**The Productive Passengers**
Use AI to think *less*. They get faster — and gradually hollowed out.

**The Reluctant Optimizers**
Know the risk, resolve to resist... then get sucked in by the rush of daily life.

**The Mental Marathoners**
Use AI to think *more* — like runners who train for miles despite the existence of cars. They wrestle with the tool to expand their own capacity.

<br>

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Today's goal: practice being marathoners, not passengers.
:::

---

## What the research shows

Brooks surveys studies suggesting the stakes are real:

- Workers who adopted AI didn't work less — their days got **fuller and more fragmented**, with less time in deep focus
- Brain-imaging studies found sharply **reduced cognitive engagement** during AI-assisted tasks
- Skills **atrophy**: physicians whose AI assistance was removed detected fewer lesions than before they'd ever used it
- People accepted an AI's deliberately planted wrong answers the **overwhelming majority** of the time

<br>

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
The tool is powerful. Passive use has a cost. So we practice *active* use.
:::

---

## What this means for education

Brooks's closing argument, and the reason this matters beyond our own workflows:

- Our system was built around **content and intelligence** — download knowledge, sort the smart. When machines know everything, that's no longer what distinguishes anyone.
- Education will have to reorient around **volition**: the desire to work hard and put knowledge to creative use
- Design matters: an AI used as an **answer machine** replaces mental muscle; an AI designed like a **tutor or personal trainer** builds it
- Motivation grows from autonomy, competence, and relatedness — and from admiration and apprenticeship
- Our courses can inflame the desire for hard thinking, or crush it

<br>

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**The goal:** avoid a future split between those who use AI to think more and those who use it to think less — starting with how *we* model it for our students.
:::

---

## Logistics (5 min)

- **Groups of 3** — one keyboard driver, one prompter, one skeptic. Rotate between activities.
- **One laptop per group** is plenty (12 groups)
- **One tool for the room:** [gemini.google.com]{.mono} — no account needed
- Get to a working chat window.

<br>

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
Skeptics: your job today is to catch the machine making mistakes. Seriously.
:::

---

# Activity 1: The Problem Set Race {background-color="#1a3a5c"}

*20 minutes · Can you get a problem set you'd actually edit and use?*

---

## Round 1 — First draft (5 min)

Adapt to any course you teach:

::: {.prompt-box}
"Create a problem set for **Calculus I** on **optimization**. Include: 4 routine problems, 3 conceptual questions that test understanding rather than computation, and 2 challenging application problems in a Latex file. In a seperate latex file Provide full worked solutions. Show me the questions first before you build the Latex files."
:::

<br>

While it generates, decide as a group: 
- **would you assign this as-is?**
- **What's wrong with it?**

::: {.prompt-box}
Finding flaws is the point — that's Round 2.
:::

---

## Round 2 — Iterate (7 min)

Pick **two** refinements and prompt for them:

1. "Problem 6 is too easy for the 'challenging' section — replace it with a related-rates twist"
2. "Rewrite the applications for the students actually in my class: [engineering / biology / economics]"
3. "Add a common-mistakes note under each solution for the grader"
4. "Check the solution to problem ___ — I think there's an error"
5. "Convert the conceptual questions to multiple choice, with distractors based on real misconceptions"

<br>

Notice: nobody needs the perfect prompt. **The conversation is the interface.**

---

## Round 3 — The make-up exam (5 min)

One prompt:

::: {.prompt-box}
"Now generate a **make-up exam version**: same structure, same difficulty, same skills tested — but different numbers and contexts, so a student who saw the original has no advantage. Include solutions."
:::

<br>

**Share-out:**

- Who got LaTeX clean enough to paste into your template?
- Who caught an actual error? What was it?
- What would you still have to do by hand?

---

# One try is not a verdict {background-color="#1a3a5c"}

*It's a first rep.*

## An invitation

Today you saw one task. Here's the ask:

**For your Fall course preparation, pick one real task from your week** — a problem set, an exam variant, a stubborn explanation, a dreaded email — **and try it with AI.**

- Bring back what you made — *or* where it broke. **Both count.**
- Want a thinking partner while you try? Paul Cannon, Ben Woodruff, Natalie Rhodes, or J. Hathaway are happy to help. Just email or ping us.
- Realize that these tools are changing every three to four weeks, criticism from two months ago often no longer apply.
- Claude Code is the premium tool for support. I recommend getting a subscription and using it.

## The final word

<br>

> "When intelligence is plentiful, volition is valuable."

<br>

<br>

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
The ground rule that outlasts today: use these tools to think *more*, not less. When intelligence is plentiful, what's valuable is the will to use it well. **We must exemplify the marathoner in our classrooms.**
:::
